title: Practice: Crude Oil and Fractional Distillation

questions.stem: In a fractionating column, crude oil is heated and the vapours rise up the column, which is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. Where would you collect diesel (boiling range 250-350°C) compared to petrol (boiling range 40-100°C)?

options.text: Diesel higher up the column than petrol
Diesel lower down the column than petrol, because it has a higher boiling point and condenses sooner
Both at the same level
Diesel at the top and petrol at the bottom

questions.explanation: Fractions with higher boiling points condense lower down the column where it is hotter. Diesel has a higher boiling range (250-350°C) so it condenses lower down. Petrol has a lower boiling range (40-100°C) and its vapour rises further up the column before condensing in the cooler region. This is how fractional distillation separates crude oil by boiling point.

questions.stem: A refinery manager notices that demand for petrol (short chains) is much higher than for bitumen (long chains). Why can they not simply distil more petrol from crude oil?

options.text: They can — they just need to heat the oil more
Fractional distillation only separates what is already present; the proportion of each fraction is fixed by the crude oil's composition
Petrol cannot be obtained from crude oil
Bitumen can be easily converted to petrol by cooling

questions.explanation: Fractional distillation is a physical separation process — it separates the mixture but does not change the molecules. The proportion of each fraction depends on the crude oil's composition. To meet the higher demand for short-chain hydrocarbons, refineries use cracking to break longer chains into shorter, more useful ones.

questions.stem: As the chain length of hydrocarbons increases, their viscosity increases (they become thicker) and they become harder to ignite. Why does this make short-chain fractions better fuels?

options.text: Short chains contain more energy per molecule
Short-chain fractions flow easily, vaporise readily, and ignite quickly, making them efficient fuels for engines
Long-chain fractions are toxic and cannot be burned
Short chains produce less carbon dioxide when burned

questions.explanation: For a fuel to work efficiently in an engine, it must flow easily through fuel lines (low viscosity), vaporise readily to mix with air (low boiling point), and ignite easily (high flammability). Short-chain hydrocarbons like petrol have all these properties. Long-chain hydrocarbons are viscous, hard to vaporise, and difficult to ignite, making them poor fuels for engines (though bitumen is used for roads).

questions.stem: Crude oil is described as a finite (non-renewable) resource. What does this mean for its long-term use?

options.text: Crude oil will last forever because new deposits are constantly forming
Crude oil is being used much faster than it forms, so supplies will eventually run out, making alternative energy sources essential
Crude oil is renewable because it comes from living organisms
We can manufacture crude oil in factories when natural supplies run out

questions.explanation: Crude oil formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient marine organisms under heat and pressure. We are using it far faster than it can form — it is a finite resource. This means we need to develop renewable alternatives (solar, wind, biofuels) and use crude oil more efficiently through recycling and reducing waste.

questions.stem: Crude oil is not just used as fuel. It provides raw materials for making plastics, medicines, and synthetic fibres. Why is burning crude oil fractions as fuel considered wasteful by some scientists?

options.text: Burning crude oil does not produce any useful energy
Once burned, the hydrocarbons are converted to CO₂ and H₂O and can never be recovered; alternative energy sources could preserve these valuable chemical feedstocks
Crude oil fractions cannot actually be used as fuels
Burning is the only possible use for crude oil

questions.explanation: Crude oil hydrocarbons are irreplaceable raw materials for the petrochemical industry (plastics, pharmaceuticals, dyes, detergents, synthetic fibres). Once burned as fuel, they are permanently converted to CO₂ and water. Since we have alternative energy sources (solar, wind, nuclear) but no alternative source of these complex organic molecules, many scientists argue we should conserve crude oil for chemical feedstock use.
